### 2023-03-15: An Entry Point Retained from a Path

The earliest page did not start with README or a confirmed instantiation name. It started with `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java`. That path was at `v_prev` in `internal/jctools-core`, and the repository index at the time described its local role in only two sentences: an existing java module, for reading code and checking historical behavior.

The public entry point was not checked at this step. This can only explain why the investigation initially started here, not prove that the type users actually receive is this base class. At the time, the options were to continue along the file's inheritance relationships and write an overview, or to separate the base file, public name, and iterator observations. The page initially chose the second option. The path was retained, the public name was left blank for the time being, and no outcome was assumed for the snapshot operation. The early record had no conclusion because there was insufficient information at the time, not because an explanation had been omitted.

### Spring 2023: Separating the File from the Name

Later addenda split the search into two tracks. The first dealt only with the file itself: the package declaration, three direct import statements, the local term `chunks`, and the revision and repository location that could be revisited for further checks. The second sought a stable public queue name. After the tracks were separated, `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java` remained the code entry point, but no longer carried the meaning of "public entry point".

This division has one practical benefit. When readers enter via a file path, they can tell that what they are seeing is a local declaration and adjacent navigation; when readers trace back from a public class name, they also will not mistake the file location for the API identity merely because the base class name appears first. Both lookup methods are retained, and they serve different evidentiary purposes.

There is still no usable completion state on the MPSC Snapshot Iterator side. The page records only the lookup method: first save the queue state before the call, perform one action, and finally compare the visible changes after completion. The presence of chunk can explain why cross-segment relationships need to be observed, but it cannot independently provide the result of the iterator action.

There was once a conclusion here that was very easy to casually write in: if chunk can be seen from the base class, the same traversal order can be used as the common basis for the public queue identity and the snapshot result. This conclusion was later retained as the old position; it was not hidden, nor was it carried forward as the current decision.

### 2024-01-05: Review addendum

During review, the following original wording was highlighted again:

> The entry point of XADD may itself be a derived type of `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue`, and changes in the snapshot iterator might perhaps be inferred from the chunk traversal order at the same location.

The review did not require it to be deleted, but required separating "possible" from "confirmed." Accordingly, the page added a local note after the old sentence: a file path supports code lookup but cannot independently support the public identity; chunk traversal can serve as a path for observation but cannot replace the actual record after the iterator completes.

This review also left a wording constraint. Without a result after completion, an open item must not be rewritten as "no change." For MPSC Snapshot Iterator, when only the pre-call state and the action have been confirmed, save only those two items; add a result only when a verifiable completion state appears. This constraint applies to the current object; it is not a general interface rule extracted from the page.

The decision after review is narrowly scoped:

1. Retain `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java` as a local code-lookup entry point;
2. Confirm the public name of XADD separately;
3. Continue treating the post-completion observation of MPSC Snapshot Iterator as an open item;
4. DOC-12 only handle atomic-generation artifacts and inheritance boundaries; they do not replace this page's entry-point assessment.

At the time, there was still no public class name to cite. As a result, this version still left the name out of the decision section and did not expand the account of cross-chunk behavior into a confirmed description of API.

### An on-the-spot review: a misreading caused by reading order

The focused review still began by looking at chunk and index relationships. This starting point is well suited to answering "what direct relationships are present in the file", but not to directly answering "what should users instantiate". The illusion created by the reading order was that, since the base class appeared to connect the chunks, the base class's inheritance relationships could be treated as evidence of public identity.

The page then unpacked this illusion. The file header and path were retained; the search terms were retained; the old identity conjecture was also retained, but marked "no longer applicable at a later stage". There were no logs proving that any additional stable change occurred after the iterator completed, so that part still contained only observation steps and unanswered questions.

This round of review produced no new implementation conclusions, but it changed the decision boundaries on the page:

- The file location can support a follow-up lookup, but not public naming;
- `chunks` can indicate what to observe, but does not establish the snapshot completion result;
- An object awaiting verification cannot borrow another object's local declaration to settle the matter prematurely.

These three points applied only to the two objects retained on this page. They were not written up as project-wide conventions or extended into judgments about other queue implementations.

### The overturned passage remains in its original place

> First, start from `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue` to examine the chunk structure of XADD, then use the traversal order from the same passage to explain MPSC Snapshot Iterator; if a chunk can be located, this path can be used as the basis for the public queue identity.

This is an early working record that was later overturned. It preserves the lookup approach used at the time and the overly strong inference, so it has not been deleted from the historical page. When reading this passage now, it should be treated as a record of a misreading: it can explain why the old page crowded three objects together, but cannot serve as evidence for the current public name, cross-chunk behavior, or iterator results.

The supplementary note from that time was retained alongside the old passage: the file path is still a valid entry point into the code, identity judgments must return to a stable public name, and post-completion observations for the iterator must be recorded separately. This treatment is closer to the page's actual revision process than polishing the old passage into the currently correct wording.

> A file can be an entry point, but that does not make it the object's identity.

> The iterator needs post-completion observations, and chunk relationships along the path cannot be used as a substitute.

The page still looked incomplete at this point. The public name still needed a stable source, and the iterator completion status still needed to be observed. The review did not fill in a speculative result simply because the page was incomplete, and decided to keep both points open.

It did not rename `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java` as a public class, and even with the appearance of a public class name, it did not fill in a completion result for MPSC Snapshot Iterator. The public name and iterator observations continued to be kept separate.

### Month 10 of 2025: The snapshot issue remains unresolved

The field description from JCT-217 placed MPSC Snapshot Iterator back in the pre-call state. The record called for reproduction to start before the call, to check whether any additional visible changes remained after completion. The addendum dated 2025-10-17 still only confirmed the current segment, and the open item remained open.

Here, "not yet confirmed" has not been rewritten as "no change". Nor has a snapshot automatically been interpreted as a continuous view, much less equated with a consumption operation. What can currently be recorded publicly is only the observation sequence: the state before the call, a single action, and a comparison after completion. If no snippet is available for the comparison result, the page leaves the item open; this is precisely the role of JCT-217 on this page.

The two live observation windows are therefore different. JCT-201 first addressed naming and queue identity, then waited for the publication window for the chunk lifecycle; JCT-217 addresses the visible changes after a single snapshot action completes, and still provides no result. Combining them into a single conclusion that "XADD has been fully confirmed" would erase the time gap between the two records and the boundaries of the issues they address.

### Entry points that can now be cited

README.md makes it clear: the public XADD queue entry points are org.jctools.queues.MpscUnboundedXaddArrayQueue and org.jctools.queues.MpmcUnboundedXaddArrayQueue; both are constructed with two int values and maintain cross-chunk FIFO, and the blocking queue still implements BlockingQueue.

This statement appears after the historical material because it describes the current public entry points added to the page only in a later version. It clarifies the two class names and the scope of their public behavior, but does not rewrite the local declarations in the base file to give them a API identity, nor does it supply the missing completion status for MPSC Snapshot Iterator.

When looking up the public entry points, start with `org.jctools.queues.MpscUnboundedXaddArrayQueue` or `org.jctools.queues.MpmcUnboundedXaddArrayQueue`. When checking the earlier file assessment, return to `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java`. Both entry points are valid, but they answer different questions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BaseFileReview
    BaseFileReview --> PublicIdentityCheck
    PublicIdentityCheck --> CrosschunkBehavior
    BaseFileReview --> MPSCSnapshotObservation
    MPSCSnapshotObservation --> CompletionStatusPendingConfirmation
    CrosschunkBehavior --> [*]
    CompletionStatusPendingConfirmation --> [*]
```

In the diagram, "Base file lookup" refers only to the path, package declaration, and direct dependencies of `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java`; "Public identity verification" refers to the two stable class names; "Cross-chunk behavior" falls within the current scope of the public entry points; "Completion status pending confirmation" refers only to the single unresolved observation for MPSC Snapshot Iterator. It is not a complete class hierarchy diagram, nor does it merge the two on-site records.

### Division of responsibilities retained in the current decision

The decision on this page is not to consolidate all the material into one overview, but to retain three adjacent but non-equivalent entry points.

**File entry point.** `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java` is responsible for local code lookup. It can be used to confirm the file-header relationships involving the `org.jctools.queues` package, `IndexedQueueSizeUtil.IndexedQueue`, `PortableJvmInfo`, and `Pow2`, and to continue reading through the context related to `chunks`. It is not responsible for providing public XADD class names.

**Public entry points.** The two XADD queue classes under `org.jctools.queues` are responsible for the identities that users can look up. The current definition of README also specifies the two-int constructor, cross-chunk FIFO, and the BlockingQueue relationship. The base class name is no longer treated as the name used for instantiation here.

**Snapshot observation entry point.** MPSC Snapshot Iterator needs to start from the pre-call state and separately record the visible changes after completion. It cannot borrow the conclusions about public queue identity, nor can it borrow the chunk relationships visible in the base file. JCT-217 still correspond to this open observation.

This division of responsibilities also explains why adjacent records cannot replace this page. DOC-12 can help review atomic-generation artifacts and inheritance boundaries, but it is not responsible for these two XADD public entry points. Conversely, this page does not bring in the details of the generator output either. Both documents retain their own subjects and lookup actions.

### How the responsibility boundaries are recorded

The core implementation side handles checking the mapping between public names and file entry points. The code path preserves only local declarations, direct dependencies, and historical lookup starting points. The review side handles separate pre-call and post-completion records for MPSC Snapshot Iterator, rather than using a queue-name conclusion in place of a single observation. The integration side brought in old links and search directions early on; when an old link led only to the base class, the page later recalibrated the entry point based on the public class name.

This is not a responsibility matrix for the entire project. The division here concerns only the two objects on this page, and it does not classify snapshot changes that have not yet been observed as completed results. The blocking record for JCT-201 still indicates a wait condition on the chunk-lifecycle side; the open item for JCT-217 still indicates that there is no existing fragment for the snapshot completion status.

### Adjacent issues still retained

"Cross-chunk FIFO" is already part of the current description of the public XADD entry, but it is not the same thing as observing MPSC Snapshot Iterator. The former has a place in the public-name and README framing, while the latter still requires a local review from before the call through completion. Just because both objects contain MPSC or chunk does not justify transferring one object's behavior to the other.

Likewise, the local dependencies of `BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java` cannot be used to fill in the public class hierarchy. The `IndexedQueue`, `PortableJvmInfo`, and `Pow2` in the file describe its direct adjacency, but they alone cannot account for all implementation details of the two XADD entry points. The generated-artifact boundary of DOC-12 also cannot be retroactively rewritten as the class identity here.

The only issue still not separated out is: after MPSC Snapshot Iterator completes the action, which changes are visible results and which are merely internal state during the action. The existing field materials do not provide a result fragment, so the issue is retained without supplying a conclusion for it.

### Appendix of legacy examples: early lookups and outdated practices

**Example 1: Start from the base class.**

```text
Input: BaseMpscLinkedArrayQueue.java
Inspect first: package, chunks, direct import
Yields: a usable code lookup entry point
Cannot directly yield: the public XADD class name
```

This example was the primary lookup method in the early period. It is still suitable today as a path entry point, but it can no longer be used to determine identity. The public names need to be traced back to README and the two stable class names; the file path preserves only local history.

**Example 2: Treating chunk traversal as the snapshot result.**

```text
Input: pre-call state for MPSC Snapshot Iterator
Old approach: after seeing the chunk relationship, directly write the traversal conclusion
Later revision: separate the state before the call, the action, and the observation after completion
```

Example 2 is outdated. It describes a misreading of a live work situation, not the result of the current operation. If it is re-verified, still start from the pre-call state and leave a snippet that can show the change after completion; if there is no snippet, continue to keep the item open.

**Example 3: Using one name to cover three kinds of objects.**

```text
Old style: the file name, public class name, and snapshot iterator were all grouped under the XADD entry
After correction: retain the path for the file, verify the public class name separately, and retain the observation window for the snapshot
```

This old example was not deleted because it explains why the page for 2023 seemed to reach closure so quickly. Later versions separated the names from the actions, leaving room to preserve the distinction between "confirmed" and "still under observation."

The examples in the appendix all retain their original temporal context. They can help readers understand how the page moved from the wrong entry point to the current one, but should not be treated as new implementation documentation. What can currently be cited reliably are the two public class names, constructor form, cross-chunk FIFO and BlockingQueue relationships provided by README; what still cannot be cited reliably is the additional visible change after the MPSC snapshot action is completed.

# Atomic Queue Generation and Cross-Chunk Review Proposal

This round, we're documenting two easily conflated issues separately: generated artifacts and inheritance boundaries for atomic queues are one track; for MPSC XADD, whether elements are still handed to consumers in production order after a chunk switch is the other. Both fall within the scope of queue-evolution-2019's interface review, but they should not share a single "passed" verdict.

The current starting point for checking back is `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/MpscAtomicArrayQueue.java`. The file header contains `package org.jctools.queues.atomic;`, and the file directly uses `PortableJvmInfo`, `AtomicLongFieldUpdater`, and `AtomicReferenceArray`. Use it as the initial reference point on the atomic array queue side; the generator's inputs, outputs, and extended uses of linked types have not yet been fully collected in this record.

I suggest starting with two samples. The generation-chain sample should answer only whether the generated class names are stable and whether callers can compile and use the files; the cross-chunk sample should observe only how producers claim positions, how slots are published, and the ordering as consumers move from the previous chunk to the next. Ordering within a single chunk is no substitute for the latter sample.

Do not document array artifacts and linked artifacts as having the same inheritance rules yet. If the generated output cannot be used, first revisit naming and template selection in the generation chain; if ordering breaks across chunks, withdraw only the FIFO assessment, without attributing the issue to the generator. Still needed: the actual generated files and a record of element order across a chunk boundary.

# Atomic Generation and Cross-Chunk Review Proposal

The previous split was useful, but an ambiguity remained during review: everyone could start investigating from the atomic array queue path, but we had not agreed on which conclusions the generation pipeline could support and which required runtime examples. As a result, "class names are visible," "generated output is usable," and "cross-chunk ordering is correct" ended up in the same paragraph. They read like a single interface assessment, but actually belong to three different levels.

`jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/MpscAtomicArrayQueue.java` remains a reference anchor. It shows the atomic package and three neighboring dependencies: `PortableJvmInfo`, `AtomicLongFieldUpdater`, and `AtomicReferenceArray`. This explains why the earlier investigation started with the atomic array queue, but this proposal no longer treats these imports as evidence for generator templates or consumer handoff.

We discussed two ways to organize this. The first was to use one generation template to describe both array and linked outputs, then append the MPSC XADD ordering examples to the template. The advantage is fewer entry points: callers only need to remember one location. The drawback is that when a compilation problem occurs, it is hard to tell whether the issue is in the generated text, the package name, or the runtime publication order. The second was to establish two verification tracks: one checks the names and generated files exposed by the generator; the other specifically constructs consumption sequences that cross a chunk boundary. The second approach retains an extra example, but makes it clear where a failure occurs.

We currently favor the second approach. The generation track first verifies the relationship between the standard entry point, the input queue source code, and the output files, then checks whether the generated files can be used as ordinary source code. The runtime track does not infer FIFO from successful generation; it records only the order of producer reservation, element writes, slot publication, and consumer handoff. If the consumer sees a slot that has not yet been published, the example should stop at the publication boundary rather than interpret an empty result as a change in ordering.

Inheritance boundaries are listed as a separate open issue. Even if linked types and array types reside in neighboring atomic packages, that does not mean they should expose the same extension mechanisms downstream. If later checks can confirm only the generated class names, not downstream usage, retain "the artifact can be located" rather than prematurely making a blanket promise of inheritance support.

Retractions follow the same boundary: if the generated files cannot compile, withdraw the instructions for integrating the generated artifacts; if the cross-chunk example cannot provide a continuous FIFO trace, withdraw the ordering assessment. Neither type of failure overrides the other. We still need to add a sample of generated output and a consumption trace covering the tail of one chunk and the start of the next.

# Atomic Generation and Cross-Chunk Review Plan

This proposal started with a lookup point for the atomic array queue. Earlier investigations used `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/MpscAtomicArrayQueue.java` for both issue names and call names, so the first draft grouped the generator, the array implementation, and cross-chunk ordering for MPSC XADD together. That made searching easier but blurred the boundaries of the interface discussion: whether a generated file is usable does not establish the element order a consumer observes during chunk rotation.

The file itself is still worth keeping in this proposal. The local neighbors visible here are `package org.jctools.queues.atomic;`, along with `PortableJvmInfo`, `AtomicLongFieldUpdater`, and `AtomicReferenceArray`. These details are enough to show that the atomic array queue is the starting point for this investigation, and explain why the array implementation and generated artifacts are often discussed together. They do not provide the full inputs to the generation template or show how a consumer moves from one chunk to the next.

The second version framed the debate as "one entry point or two examples." It retained two candidate structures. The combined version centered on the generation template, with ordering examples as an additional check after the template; the split version first pinned down the generation pipeline's public artifacts, then covered cross-chunk FIFO scenarios separately. The former meant one fewer thing to maintain, but a single conclusion would obscure both compilation failures and ordering failures. The latter required keeping two separate sets of material, but would let us limit changes to either the generation pipeline or the runtime path when a problem arose.

This revision still uses the split structure, but does not require both tracks to produce the same results at the same time. The generation pipeline needs to answer whether the entry point can be invoked, whether the generated filenames are stable, and whether the generated artifacts can be incorporated into the caller as source code. The cross-chunk track needs to answer when an element is written to its slot after the producer claims a position, when it is published, and how the last element in the previous chunk relates to the first element in the next chunk when the consumer crosses the boundary. If the former fails, check the inputs, outputs, and generated text first; if the latter fails, preserve the reservation, publication, and handoff positions first, without treating generator success as validation.

The early draft also made an unwarranted inference: seeing adjacent array and linked names in the atomic package, it assumed they offered downstream users the same inheritance options. That assumption has been dropped. Whether the array artifact is used directly and whether the linked type is suitable as a base class for extension are different questions. Package location no longer stands in for actual declarations or caller results here; until we have seen downstream integration, "can be generated" will not be written as "any queue can be subclassed."

The text slated to remain in the release notes is:

> README.md explicitly states: the two stable artifacts of the atomic generation pipeline are org.jctools.queues.atomic.MpscAtomicArrayQueue and org.jctools.queues.atomic.MpscLinkedAtomicQueue; the generator provides a main entry point, and the linked type can be subclassed downstream.

This sentence groups the artifacts and inheritance boundaries because they belong to the generation pipeline's external interface, not because the array and linked implementations have the same runtime semantics. `main` should be rechecked as a generator entry point: it takes an output directory and input queue source code and generates the corresponding source files. Callers care about stable artifact names and usability; they do not need to reconstruct the generation process from the import list in `MpscAtomicArrayQueue.java`.

The MPSC XADD section remains a separate behavioral proposal. Examples must actually cross a chunk boundary; the order of filling and draining a single chunk is not a substitute. At a minimum, the record should allow us to distinguish the position reserved by the producer, the slot actually written to, the consumer-visible publication point, and the position of the handoff to the next chunk. When an element has been written but not published, the fact that the consumer has not retrieved it does not automatically mean FIFO is wrong; only after the consumer has crossed the boundary do we need to compare the order in which adjacent elements from the two chunks are consumed.

This also changes how failures are handled. If the generated artifacts cannot compile or the entry-point contract is unclear, withdraw the generation pipeline's integration notes and retain the atomic array queue path as a lookup point. If the cross-chunk examples lack continuous FIFO evidence, withdraw the ordering conclusion for MPSC XADD and keep a record of whether the failure occurred near reservation, publication, or handoff. If there is still no material showing downstream use of the linked type, do not broaden the inheritance commitment or drop that open question just because the array artifact works.

JCT-202 is for continuing work to identify the atomic generation artifacts and inheritance boundaries; JCT-218 is for collecting cross-chunk ordering examples. The results should be added back to the two cards separately: add the actual generated files and caller compilation results to the former, and the relationships between adjacent elements in boundary-crossing sequences to the latter. If later work confirms only the names and entry point, this proposal will stop with the generation pipeline closed out and runtime ordering still awaiting examples, rather than collapsing the two levels into a single release decision.

# OSGi package exports and XADD troubleshooting tree

Initially, only two symptoms were noted side by side: the built core package was not visible in the runtime environment; results with multiple consumers were unstable after crossing a chunk boundary. Both were put on the same troubleshooting note at the time, but it had not yet been confirmed whether they shared an entry point.

First, preserve the original error message. If all you have is a paraphrase such as "package not found" or "queue error," don't assign ownership.

```text
Build or loading error
├─ Artifact is missing manifest information
└─ Artifact has the information but is still not visible in the runtime environment

Queue consumption error
├─ Single consumer
└─ Multiple consumers, with problems appearing after crossing a chunk boundary
```

The source-code entry point still being used at the time was:

`jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java`

The file header shows `org.jctools.queues.atomic`, `IndexedQueue`, `PortableJvmInfo`, and `Pow2`. That is enough as a starting point for reading the atomic-queue code, but not enough to establish the actual queue type used by multiple consumers or the manifest details in the build artifact.

# OSGi Package Exports and XADD Troubleshooting Tree

2024-11-28 addendum. The previous version put build/loading issues and cross-chunk consumption in the same tree, which made it easy to keep following the same source link during troubleshooting. This version keeps that entry point but splits the two paths.

## Old Entry Point

The early notes pointed to:

`jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java`

The file header at the time showed:

`package org.jctools.queues.atomic;`

`import org.jctools.queues.IndexedQueueSizeUtil.IndexedQueue;`

`import org.jctools.util.PortableJvmInfo;`

`import org.jctools.util.Pow2;`

Following these names to nearby index, capacity, and runtime code does lead to an actual source file. The old notes then linked "near an atomic queue" with "multi-consumer use," but that step wasn't sufficiently supported. The MPSC in the filename is no substitute for the caller identifying the actual queue type, either.

## Routing

First check where the error comes from. If you have build artifacts or container loading information, take the manifest branch; if you have enqueue order, consumption results, or regression output, take the queue branch. If you have neither, just save the original text.

```text
An anomaly is reported
│
├─ Has JAR, container logs, or a package-not-visible message
│  ├─ Manifest information is missing
│  │  └─ Stop at the artifact; record the JAR used
│  └─ Manifest information is present but the package is still not visible
│     └─ Also record the runtime environment and package name
│
└─ Has a queue call site or consumption output
   ├─ Queue type is unknown
   │  └─ Go back to the caller for the class name and version
   ├─ Only one consumer
   │  └─ Do not classify as a multi-consumer case
   └─ Multiple consumers and anomalous results
      └─ Save the order, results, and cross-chunk location
```

## Limits Established by the Review

One review confirmed only the package declaration and three direct imports in the file above; that local snippet did not establish a direct link to a multi-consumer queue. The statement "the index path in the atomic base class is enough to explain the anomaly" is therefore retained, but should be marked as an old assessment and no longer used as a routing rule.

Likewise, the source package name is no substitute for checking the build artifact. If all you have is a Java file path, record it as source navigation; if the runtime reports that a package is not visible, also save the container's original message and the manifest information from the artifact. Do not conflate the two.

We once tried categorizing all cross-chunk anomalies by capacity calculations first, then going back to find the consumers. This left no record of the caller, consumer count, or actual queue type, so we could not later determine whether it was a single-consumer observation or a multi-consumer issue. That sequence has been abandoned.

## Available Actions

- Build side: Get the actual JAR and save the relevant manifest text verbatim; do not assess the build result without JAR.
- Runtime side: Copy down the package name reported by the container and the artifact used; if the package name is missing, keep the original "not visible" message.
- Queue side: Confirm the actual type from the caller, then record the enqueue order, consumption results, and consumer count.
- Boundary: If the cross-chunk location has not been observed, write not located; do not specify an index or slot.

This page remains a historical troubleshooting record; it does not assign responsibility for the current multi-consumer behavior to the atomic MPSC file.

# OSGi Package Exports and XADD Troubleshooting Tree

This page starts from a somewhat unreliable entry point. Someone first saw "the core package is not visible in the runtime environment", then saw "results are wrong when multiple consumers cross a chunk boundary", so they placed the two terms beside the same source code link. The link has remained to this day, while later additions keep pointing out: this has not been proven to be a shared failure.

## 2024-02-08: First record the files that can be opened

The earliest record contained only one path and a few lines of guidance:

`jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java`

The file header shows:

`package org.jctools.queues.atomic;`

`import org.jctools.queues.IndexedQueueSizeUtil.IndexedQueue;`

`import org.jctools.util.PortableJvmInfo;`

`import org.jctools.util.Pow2;`

The idea at the time was straightforward: if the anomaly was near an atomic queue, start with this base class to check the indices and capacity; if container loading also failed, check the package name along the way. The advantage of this approach was that it did not stop at a vague issue title, and immediately provided a file to open. The downside was that it placed objects from different layers too close together.

The branches in the early note were as follows, kept just as brief as the original:

```text
Anomaly
├─ Container side: first check package names and build artifacts
└─ Queue side: first check indices, capacity, and chunk crossings
```

No actual caller, consumer count, or build artifact excerpt was available at the time. So this was only an opening step, not an attribution of cause. In particular, you cannot infer directly from MPSC in the filename that the queue used by multiple consumers is the one at this path.

## 2024-03-01: A sentence added in the on-call margin

Later, someone wrote next to the original entry point: "First ask whether the name in the error is a bundle name, a package name, or a queue class name." This sentence was short, but it changed the troubleshooting order.

If what you have is JAR or container logs, first save the original text and the artifact's identity. Having only a source path means, at most, that you can start reading here; it does not tell you what the runtime environment read. If the issue description says that a package is not visible, record the package name separately; the bundle name and exported packages are not the same thing.

If what you have is a call site or regression output, first copy down the actual queue class name, then ask for the number of consumers. Use the "multiple consumers" branch only when multiple consumers have already been recorded. Record the corresponding behavior only when the output identifies the enqueue order, consumption results, or the location of a chunk crossing.

The on-call margin note also left a stopping condition: when all you have is "the queue does not work", do not derive a conclusion from `IndexedQueue`, `Pow2`, or the filename. A missing object identity cannot be replaced by a nearby name.

## 2024-04-17: An unsuccessful recheck

The recheck followed the old approach of examining index-related adjacency from `IndexedQueue`, then examining the capacity semantics of `Pow2`. In the end, it still yielded only the local declarations of this base class in the atomic package, not the direct call relationships for consumption by multiple consumers in MPMC.

This attempt failed not because these names were irrelevant, but because the question needed to answer "why consumption by multiple consumers was behaving abnormally", while the available material provided only a local view of a MPSC base class. Capacity, indexing, element publication, and consumer handoff were therefore written into a single paragraph, making them look connected, when in fact there was no evidence from callers.

The recheck notes also pointed out a similar misreading in the manifest branch: the Java package in the source code can help locate files, but it cannot be used to determine what symbolic name the built JAR uses in the container, nor can it prove which packages have already been exported. This boundary was not made clear at the time, so the old links continued to be used afterward.

At the time, there was an attempt to first attribute all cross-chunk anomalies to "array capacity calculation". The queue class name and consumer count were not saved, so the second person who took over could not reproduce the same branch. That attempt is retained here as a working method that has already failed; do not automatically interpret "cross-chunk" as a capacity issue again.

## 2024-11-28: Review addendum, old conclusions retained

During the review of this version, the debate focused on "whether the old entry point should be removed". In the end it was not removed, because the names used for issues and calls could still lead readers to that file. Keeping the link does not mean keeping the old attribution.

The review margin note said:

> You can start from the old file to check the historical navigation, but before assessing the current issue you must return to the actual artifact or actual caller.

Therefore, the old entry "the index path in the atomic base class is sufficient to explain queue anomalies" remains in the history section, and is marked as deprecated here. It describes the working habits of the time, not a current operational conclusion.

This time, the minimum required evidence for the two branches was also specified more concretely: the build side requires at least the actual JAR, the original manifest text or the package name in the container error; the queue side requires at least the caller, actual type, consumer count or consumption results. When the evidence is incomplete, record the gaps, rather than borrowing a name from the other side to fill them.

## Old troubleshooting tree (retained version)

The tree below comes from an early version of the page, and its structure is still usable, but the "atomic base class" at the leaves only indicates a navigation entry point.

```text
Error received
│
├─ A bundle, manifest or package visibility issue appears first
│  ├─ No actual JAR
│  │  └─ Save only the container error message, and stop assessing the manifest
│  ├─ JAR is available but there is no verbatim header text
│  │  └─ Stop at artifact inspection, and record what is missing
│  └─ The header has been saved but the package is still not visible
│     └─ Also record the package name and the runtime environment messages
│
└─ Unexpected consumption results appear first
   ├─ No actual queue class name
   │  └─ Return to the caller, and do not classify based on filenames
   ├─ There is one consumer
   │  └─ Retain the single-consumer observation, and exit the multi-party branch
   ├─ Multiple consumers have been confirmed but the results have not been saved
   │  └─ Add the enqueue order and consumption results
   └─ Multiple consumers and unexpected results have both been recorded
      └─ Then record whether crossing chunk boundaries was actually observed
```

The tree does not connect the build branch and the consumption branch. They can appear in the same pre-release check, but there is currently no evidence that one causes the other.

## After 2025-09-22: Build-side investigation entry point

JCT-203 was later used as a build-side navigation point, with the goal of tracing the build logs to find the actual steps for the manifest and package exports. This entry point addresses "which step generated or retained the build information", and is not a replacement for artifact inspection.

When entering this branch, first have the actual build artifact, the verbatim manifest visible in the build steps, the package name reported by the runtime environment, and information on whether the artifact is the same version used by the runtime environment. Old links in the directory alone are not enough to confirm these four items. Do not describe old links in a regular directory, restricted access to detail pages and container loading failures as the same symptom either.

If there is only a secondhand report that "the package cannot be found", without JAR or the verbatim container message, JCT-203 can help locate the build steps, but cannot be used to confirm the export results. At this point, troubleshooting should stop at the missing artifact or missing error message, and must not go back to treating source paths as evidence of artifacts.

## After 2025-10-17: Queue-side investigation entry point

JCT-219 point to regression locations that still exercise multi-consumer behavior. This requires checking the actual version, entry point, and current results. This navigation is more narrowly scoped than the earlier "when you see XADD, trace from the base class" and points more directly to a target that can be rechecked.

After locating the caller, follow the tree below:

```text
Locate the queue caller
│
├─ The actual type differs from the old record
│  └─ Keep the old record as a historical sample, and start a new record based on the actual type
├─ The type matches but there is only one consumer
│  └─ Exit the multi-consumer branch, and retain the single-consumer result
├─ Multiple consumers are involved and the results are normal
│  └─ Record the version and entry point, and do not treat the old failure sample as a current failure
└─ Multiple consumers are involved and the results are abnormal
   ├─ Enqueue order and consumption results are available
   │  └─ Distinguish between loss, duplication, or changes in order
   └─ One of these is missing
      └─ Stop at the regression materials, and add the raw output
```

Only use cross-chunk when the materials actually identify a boundary. If it is merely a search term in the issue title, record it as not yet located; do not assign a slot, index, or responsibility for rotation just to close out the branch.

## An explanation that was overturned

The old page once treated "there is no problem with the source package name" as a sign that the manifest was roughly correct, and also treated "atomic array queue" as the default entry point for cross-chunk multi-consumer behavior. Both statements are retained because people arriving via the old issue name will still see them; both have now been narrowed to historical judgments.

The source package is used to locate Java files. The built JAR has its own separate manifest. What the runtime environment sees is, in turn, the result of combining the artifact and export information. The same applies on the queue side: a file path can provide a starting point for reading, but it cannot establish which queue the caller actually uses. Without a call edge, do not identify `BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java` as the file responsible for this anomaly.

## Review excerpts: when to stop

Subsequent reviews did not add any new implementation conclusions based on this source path, but only made the stopping conditions stricter:

- Without the actual JAR, stop discussing bundle names and package exports;
- Without the original manifest text, stop using the source package to infer the build result;
- Without a call site and queue type, stop calling the issue MPMC XADD;
- Without the consumer count, stop using "multi-consumer behavior" to explain duplication or loss;
- Without a cross-chunk observation point, stop describing the issue as a boundary rotation failure.

These conditions do not require collecting materials from both sides every time. Records that only concern the build stay on the build side; records that only concern consumption stay on the queue side. What they jointly constrain is cross-layer inference, rather than requiring this old page to be turned into one large table.

## Current manifest guidance

Following the early entry points, on-call side notes, failure rechecks, and subsequent reviews, the build side currently follows the explicit guidance below. README.md states explicitly: the OSGi manifest for jctools-core uses Bundle-SymbolicName, fixes the symbolic value at org.jctools.core, and exports the queues, atomic, and util packages.

This guidance only specifies the header, symbolic value, and scope of package exports to check in the build artifact. After obtaining the actual JAR, you still need to save its manifest and confirm that this JAR is the artifact actually used by the runtime environment. If the header and export information match this guidance but the container still refuses to load it, keep the issue on the runtime environment branch; do not go back to the atomic queue source code to look for a manifest-related cause.

If the header is missing, the symbolic value does not match, or the exported packages are incomplete, first record the build artifact issue separately. At this point, do not attribute the queue-side MPMC behavior to the same cause. Both types of issues may appear during the same release check, but this page provides no evidence linking them in a causal chain.

## Current troubleshooting tree

The version below was added later. It is placed after the history section to make it easier to branch by investigation target when arriving via an old link.

```text
Anomaly detected before release
│
├─ The observed issue comes from JAR, manifest or container loading
│  ├─ The actual JAR is missing
│  │  └─ Save the original container output and stop assessing the artifact contents
│  ├─ JAR is present, but the header is missing or the symbol value does not match
│  │  └─ Save the artifact source and header, and check back through the build steps
│  ├─ The header is correct but the required package is not exported
│  │  └─ Save the package name and export information, and continue checking on the build side
│  └─ Both the header and exports meet the agreed criteria
│     └─ Retain the container error and switch to the runtime environment branch
│
└─ The observed issue comes from consumption results for a queue that has been run
   ├─ The caller or version is missing
   │  └─ Go to JCT-219 to find the actual entry point
   ├─ The caller is known but the consumer count is unknown
   │  └─ Record only a consumption anomaly, not consumption by multiple parties
   ├─ Multiple consumers are confirmed but the results have not been saved
   │  └─ Add the order, results and boundary observations
   └─ Both multiple consumers and anomalous results are confirmed
      ├─ Cross-chunk positions have been observed
      │  └─ Record the specific result categories and boundary positions
      └─ Cross-chunk positions have not been observed
         └─ Keep it marked as not yet localized, without attributing responsibility to an implementation
```

## Current requirements are listed here

After at least several earlier rounds of old records and corrections, the current requirement on the queue side is: to claim that MPMC XADD Multi-Consumer is anomalous, you must first have the actual call entry point, queue identity, consumer count and result evidence. If the entry point is missing, an old filename cannot be used in its place; if the consumer count is missing, "multiple parties" cannot be used in its place; if results are missing, the term cross-chunk cannot be used in their place.

To enter the current regression branch for JCT-219, retain the actual version, entry point and current results. JCT-219 has entered review, but that does not mean this page can declare all environments stable on its behalf. If the submission order, consumption results or boundary positions have not been saved, the record still remains at the insufficient-evidence stage.

The same applies on the build side. The navigation notes for JCT-203 can help locate the build steps for the manifest and package exports, but confirmation of interface compatibility must not be inflated into a finalized build decision. Only once the artifact, header, package name and container message are each in their proper place, can you proceed to determine the next step.

## Issues still set aside

This page still has one unresolved adjacent issue that has not been split out: whether the objects referenced by the source code and the package exports of the build artifacts are always consistent across different usage sites. It sits next to the manifest check, but it is not the direct answer to any particular container-loading failure; nor can it be inferred from the MPMC regression result. It is being retained for now because the old entry point brought these two directions together; deleting it would make the historical path look neater than it actually is.

If this issue is documented separately in the future, it should start with a specific build artifact and a specific usage site; do not start again from the broad heading "queue anomaly." For now, this page retains it only as an unresolved adjacent item.

## Appendix: Excerpts from Old Meetings

The two passages below were not deleted because they explain why the old links persisted for so long. They no longer serve as the order of operations.

> First check the index in the atomic queue base class; if the source package name is fine, the manifest is probably fine too; revisit multiple consumers later.

The first sentence can still serve as historical navigation. The second was later overturned: the source package cannot confirm the manifest. The third indicates that there was no material about multiple consumers at the time, rather than constituting an actionable decision to defer.

Another old note says: "Cross-chunk behavior is, by definition, a rotation issue." This no longer applies either. Cross-chunk behavior is merely a boundary description that needs to be located; without the number of consumers, the dispatch order, and the actual results, these few words cannot support conclusions about loss, duplication, or FIFO.

The final note left next to the appendix was: "Do not overwrite the old paragraphs; append new material afterward." Consequently, this page does not look like a guide written all at once, but the old judgments, the directions later corrected, and the objects that still need to be carried forward can all still be found.

# Generation Paths and relaxedPoll Decision Record

Old links still use this record as an entry point for two adjacent issues: what text a generation operation leaves behind for long-term comparison, and how MPMC's relaxedPoll should not be interpreted as allowing indefinite spinning on an empty read. The first draft placed them side by side so that both would be visible in a single requirements inventory; when the scope was revisited later, this juxtaposition also led to a misreading, as though both issues could be resolved in one place in the atomic array queue code.

The purpose of retaining this old decision is not to turn it into an overview of queue behavior. It preserves the choices made at the time: directories belong to the execution environment, while target filenames are appropriate for stable records; a read that retrieves no element also does not directly imply that the consumer should continue occupying the processor. These two statements apply to different subjects and have different review entry points.

## The Two Options in the First Draft

Generator output was originally recorded in two ways: with the full location or with just the filename. The benefit of the full location was practical: a single line of the run record told you which directory contained the artifact, saving one navigation step during ad hoc troubleshooting. Its problems were equally clear. Working directories, temporary directories, and machine-specific path segments are not the generated artifact itself; once included in long-term materials, they make identical generation results look different and can mislead later readers into believing that the directory layout is an external contract.

Filename-only records sacrificed this ability to locate the artifact immediately. Finding where execution took place still required returning to the execution environment or the materials from that run, but the text recording successful generation could be compared by target file. The first draft chose this narrower approach: stable records identify the generated file, without treating the output directory as identifying information. This choice does not extend to the generator's input parameters, source package names, or build directories, nor does it mean that no log may contain a path. Paths may still appear where temporary files or execution locations need to be diagnosed; this decision only addresses the record left for reference after successful generation.

The compromise of "save it in full first, then strip the prefix when archiving" was not adopted at the time. Stripping the prefix sounded like it retained the benefits of both approaches, but there was no common rule for who would decide which part belonged to the environment and which part was part of the input. Letting each entry point trim it independently would make stability depend on the habits of whoever wrote the record. By contrast, using the target filename directly as the long-term identifier was narrower in scope, but its boundary needed no further explanation.

The discussion of MPMC also included a similar option that was easy to confuse with the intended one: defining no spinning as retrying empty reads a fixed number of times. This version was not adopted. No material showed that a fixed number could represent all MPMC use cases; The bigger issue is the retry count, backoff, and yielding the processor are choices for a specific read path and should not be implicitly settled through this requirements history. The only judgment retained was a lower-level one: an empty read by relaxedPoll does not imply continuous spinning by default.

## Boundaries Deliberately Kept Separate at the Time

Generator records address what the materials expose. They concern how the same generation operation can leave comparable text across different directories and execution environments. MPMC relaxedPoll addresses what the consumer does when a read retrieves no element. It concerns the read state and the waiting method. Both can appear in a regression-testing inventory, but they do not share a single behavioral boundary.

There was a proposal to combine them into "generated queue regression": as long as the generated output was stable, consumer reads would also be considered covered. This merger was not included in the decision. A change to the generator's record format does not show that MPMC's read behavior has changed; conversely, a regression run for a read path cannot verify whether the output text leaks the execution directory. Tying both to the same result makes it impossible, on failure, to know whether to investigate the generation entry point or the consumer path first.

The first draft also contained a rough working assumption: the atomic array queue was close to the generated artifacts, so it could conveniently serve as the main entry point for assessing MPMC. This assumption was later narrowed. It explains why the early notes placed the two names together, but it did not become evidence of where the implementation belonged. The old links have not been cleaned up, so this misreading is not being removed either.

> Old judgment: the atomic array queue file can be used to complete the review of both the generator and MPMC.
>
> This statement later ceased to apply. The file's location only provides an entry point into the atomic array queue side; MPMC's read behavior still has to be assessed through the corresponding consumer paths and execution results.

## File Adjacency Observed During the Review

The atomic array queue section is still accessible through `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/MpscAtomicArrayQueue.java`. The file is in the `org.jctools.queues.atomic` package, and its header contains direct imports of `org.jctools.util.PortableJvmInfo`, `java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLongFieldUpdater`, and `java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReferenceArray`. This adjacency information is useful for checking where the generated atomic array queue resides and which atomic fields and array objects a reader encounters first.

This information cannot make the MPSC atomic array queue a substitute for evidence of MPMC behavior. In particular, relaxedPoll's looping behavior cannot be inferred solely from a package name, class name, or import list. In the first draft, "atomic" was treated as a shared technical justification for the two requirements; after review, it was retained only as a description of code adjacent to the generated artifacts. This correction did not change the original choice about output records, nor did it supply a waiting strategy for MPMC.

The generator side should also avoid another overextension: a filename-only success record is not a directory navigation feature. If troubleshooting requires knowing where execution took place, the directory should be found in materials from the execution environment; a stable record cannot be expected to pinpoint the location on the machine, identify the artifact, and explain the call chain all at once. Mixing all three into one line is precisely why the early full-path format later proved difficult to compare.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> GeneratorOutput
    GeneratorOutput: Generator output
    GeneratorOutput --> TargetFileName
    TargetFileName: Target filename record
    [*] --> MpmcRelaxedPoll
    MpmcRelaxedPoll: MPMC relaxedPoll
    MpmcRelaxedPoll --> NoSpinReview
    NoSpinReview: No-spin review
```

The diagram preserves only the way the paths were separated at the time. It does not indicate that the two branches share an implementation, nor that either branch has already specified all runtime conditions.

## Old Statements Still Retained After Review

Another early formulation was "no spinning is equivalent to returning immediately". This statement is also retained in the old materials, but can no longer serve as the decision here. No spinning only rules out repeated empty reads as the default means of waiting; it does not stipulate that a given call will necessarily return immediately, nor does it replace publication state, consumer handoff, or other queue conditions. This distinction is retained to prevent an empty read from being mistakenly classified as a generator-record issue.

Similarly, some early descriptions turned "record only the filename" into "no record should contain a path". That claim was too broad. Compilation, temporary file handling, and local diagnostics may still need directory information. The decision actually retained is narrower: stable records of successful generation do not use the output directory as identifying information. If a full directory path still appears in the old materials, first determine whether it belongs to a temporary diagnostic record, rather than immediately treating it as a counterexample to the generator convention.

This page therefore preserves two historical passages whose scope has since been narrowed, rather than erasing them and replacing them with a single current slogan. The old judgments explain why the early regression notes placed paths, atomic array queues, and MPMC reads next to each other; the later corrections limit what can be inferred from that proximity.

## Later Maintenance Entry Points

JCT-206 records Generator Output Path Privacy's current inventory of dependents. This entry point went through document review first, then moved into actual work. It requires starting at the repository root and retaining the final list of matches, and can be used to find places that still depend on the old output format; this decision does not supply its match results.

JCT-222, meanwhile, is MPMC relaxedPoll Spin-Free's maintenance entry point, and maintenance ownership has been confirmed. The card requires triggering the corresponding job through the existing automation entry point and recording the job, commit, and actual artifact name. The results of that job are not restated here as a complete conclusion about MPMC; this only explains why that job and generator output records cannot be treated as the same verification.

DOC-17 discusses the unpublished-state boundaries for pooled chunk Rotation Diagnostics and MPSC relaxedPeek. It shares this page's context of neighboring topics from a single requirements inventory, but does not carry forward this page's generator-record decision. For chunk rotation or peek issues, return to DOC-17; this page's old wording about relaxedPoll must not replace the boundaries on that page.

## What Remains in This Decision

Only three decisions can still be recovered from this page: long-term records of successful generation use the target file as the identifier; the no-spin requirement for MPMC relaxedPoll must be handled independently; the atomic array queue source code is only a starting point for reading the code on the generated-artifact side. No generator directory parameters were set here, no retry count was specified for MPMC, and no single regression procedure was prescribed for all queue types.

This record is no longer a complete maintenance guide, but old links still lead here. When reading "complete the review in the same place" or "no spinning means returning immediately", treat them as former working judgments, not as rules to keep extending.

# Atomic Resize Reservation Rollback Migration Procedure

This page retains the earlier migration approach. It is not about restructuring the queue implementation into new layers, but about moving compatibility checks from temporary caller-side markers to a fixed code entry point. At the time, this was expected to reduce repeated checks. The entry point is still `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/atomic/BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java`.

The original migration diagram has not been changed:

```text
Old: caller-side failure marker -> manually check whether the reservation is still held

New: caller-side failure marker -> BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java
                              |
                              +-> inspect the failure branch
                              +-> assume the reservation has been released
```

At the time, "migrating" did not mean moving classes or renaming packages. The caller still retained the state from before the failure; only the post-failure check was shifted to a code-reading path around this base class. The old record described atomic resizing and reservation release as one continuous operation: enter resizing, acquire a producer reservation, reclaim the reservation if resizing does not complete, and only then let the caller continue. This page follows that historical interpretation of the steps as one continuous operation.

## Procedure Used at the Time

1. Start from the pre-call state. First mark the attempt that caused the resize not to complete; do not start by inferring the outcome from the queue size. The old approach required retaining the temporary caller-side marker until a lookup along the base-class path was complete.
2. Open `BaseMpscLinkedAtomicArrayQueue.java` and read down from the package declaration `org.jctools.queues.atomic`. The migration check treats this only as a shared reference point for atomic array queues, without creating a separate caller checklist.

It helped focus attention on the producer side at the time, but narrowed the observable outcome too much. Now treat it only as a provisional hypothesis about the observed state, pending retirement: whether the index returns to the position before acquisition is not the same question as whether it still occupies the position for a subsequent production after failure. The review input remains the same type of scenario: bring the producer to the point where a resize is required while maintaining the condition that prevents the resize from completing. Split the record into two parts; do not collapse them into "the queue did not get stuck." If it fails again, record whether the failure appears in the same way; if it can proceed, record whether the new element can be retrieved by the consumer. The fact that previously published elements can still be retrieved shows only that the corresponding published state remains visible; it does not show that the producer reservation from the failed operation has been released. Do not attribute the ordering issue directly to reservation rollback just because both occur around resizing.

# Blocking take Interrupt Recovery Trial Plan

The initial draft limited the scope to exits from a blocking `take`, to avoid turning this issue into changes across the entire queue interface. Review still starts at `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue.java`: the file is in package `org.jctools.queues`, and the visible local context includes `AbstractQueue`, `Iterator`, and `LockSupport`. These names only identify the adjacent locations inspected in this review; they do not replace a section-by-section assessment of the wait path.

Later, JCT-212 was added for navigation. The observation recorded when the card was created was "take interrupt recovery output cannot be reproduced consistently". That changed the original plan to choose an approach straight away: failing to reproduce it once does not prove that the exit state is intact, and one incidental recovery does not prove that nothing was left behind. We'll first record interrupt timing separately from whether operations can continue after exit, then decide where to make the change.

## Proposed Semantics

This trial uses a reviewable acceptance criterion rather than judging by whether "the thread has woken up": `interrupted take must clear its blocked reservation`. Here, blocked reservation means the local reservation left by a waiting operation that affects subsequent handoffs; it does not mean treating arbitrary producer state as part of consumer interrupt handling.

Candidate A routes all exits that return from the wait region and have not yet completed the element handoff through the same cleanup logic. Its appeal is that interrupts and other early returns would no longer each have their own cleanup action. The risk is also clear: if the handoff has already completed after a normal wakeup, converging the exits must not cause the state to be processed again.

Candidate B leaves the successful return path unchanged and handles this reservation only at confirmed interrupt exits. It is better suited to a narrow change, but only if all possible interrupt exits have been identified; miss one, and the issue will still appear with different timing. The preference is to first verify whether A can clearly distinguish "handoff completed" from "handoff not completed", and fall back to B if it cannot. This preference is intended to reduce missed exits, not to make a claim about the existing control flow.

## Trial Data Collection

The minimal scenario uses one blocking `take` on an empty queue. Record the results separately for interrupts before entering the wait, after the thread has parked, and around the point where the wait returns. For each scenario, check only four things: whether the call leaves the wait due to the interrupt, whether the waiter actually exits, the relevant index readings before and after exit, and whether one subsequent producer operation and one consumer operation can complete. Also keep a normal wakeup without an interrupt as a control, so differences in normal wakeup behavior are not attributed to the interrupt branch.

Index readings should not serve as a conclusion on their own. The relevant raw producer-index observations are in DOC-23; this page only needs them to determine whether a candidate leaves behind the reservation from the blocking period. If only interrupts "after parking" can be reproduced consistently, keep the change scoped to that path and record interrupts before waiting as another return behavior to be checked. If the issue cannot be reproduced at any of the three timings, leave the gap and do not fill in a cause.

## Post-Review Trade-offs

We do not recommend starting with a broad restructuring to unify all wait exits. This queue file also has regular queue-interface code nearby; expanding the scope of the changes would make a single interrupt-recovery trial hard to interpret. Start with a local implementation that makes the differences between exits visible: paths that successfully obtain an element must not enter interrupt cleanup; only wait paths known to exit due to an interrupt should check whether the reservation has been cleared. A's value is in making this boundary visible in one place; B's is in leaving the successful path unchanged. The final choice depends on whether the current branch can make that distinction.

Nor does "an exception was thrown" count as a pass. If the caller can receive the interrupt but the next operation can no longer make progress, that is still a failure; conversely, a change in index readings alongside continued progress in subsequent production and consumption is not enough on its own to declare it fixed. The inconsistent behavior in JCT-212 therefore remains a constraint on the trial, rather than being recast as an established cause of the failure.

## Rollback Conditions

Roll back the candidate change immediately if it prevents a wait that was not interrupted from completing via its original path. Also roll it back if the next producer or consumer operation after an interrupt cannot proceed, and retain the record for that timing. If A requires handling completed and incomplete handoff states in the same section of code, do not keep forcing the exits to converge; try B instead. If B still cannot enumerate all interrupt exits, stop changing the code and return to reviewing the wait and return paths in the file.
