# Blocking Queue Index Troubleshooting Tree

"The index did not move" appeared several times in the on-call notes. It later became clear that this phrase conflated three different things: a read operation, a description of the state while waiting, and an attribution to the producer side. The old page initially treated this as the producer side not advancing. That wording is retained because it genuinely represented the starting point for investigation at the time; it can no longer be treated as a result.

An investigation can start from any of the following symptoms, but each branch must stop where the evidence is insufficient:

- The consumer still has not returned, and the report includes only one index value;
- The report says the index was the same before and after, but does not give the times of the two reads;
- The code location is described as a blocking queue, but the actual class name has not yet been checked;
- The read operation and the description that "the thread is waiting" come from different records and cannot be placed in order.

Record the object first, then where the read occurs. If the object name has not been checked, keep it as a "candidate object"; do not treat the candidate class as an established fact about the incident. If the call site, the read timing, or the result the user actually saw is missing, all subsequent judgments must remain at the symptom level.

```text
Report of "index not moving" received
├─ No call site
│  ├─ Only one numeric value
│  │  └─ Record the reader and timing; stop attributing a cause
│  ├─ A description says "the consumer is waiting"
│  │  └─ Save the waiting description separately from the read record
│  └─ The operation sequence can be filled in
│     └─ Label Before waiting / While waiting / After waiting
├─ Call site available, but class name not checked
│  ├─ Points to MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue
│  │  └─ Open the source entry point and check the object being read
│  └─ Points to another queue or wrapper layer
│     └─ Stop at the actual class name; do not carry over this page's judgments
├─ Class name checked
│  ├─ Only one sampling point
│  │  └─ Keep the value and request adjacent operations
│  ├─ Two sampling points, no intervening operations
│  │  └─ Keep their order; do not interpret equality or change
│  └─ Sampling points and adjacent operations available
│     └─ Then determine whether they are actually at a wait boundary
└─ Timing still unknown
   └─ Write "Unknown"; do not fill in guesses
```

## Which Entry Point to Start From

Both the old troubleshooting notes and this review point to:

`jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue.java`

The file belongs to `org.jctools.queues`, and the direct dependencies visible at the top of the file include `java.util.AbstractQueue`, `java.util.Iterator`, and `java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport`. These names only help locate the relevant code to read. `AbstractQueue` cannot replace a record of the actual queue operations, and `Iterator` does not establish that an observation from iteration represents blocking progress; the presence of `LockSupport` does not mean that parking or a wakeup had definitely already occurred in a particular incident.

After opening the file, first check whether the object in the report belongs to this class, then review the local code on either side of the read. Do not skip the class-name check just because the report contains MPSC, blocking, or progress. The old notes located this path using the issue name and call name, but the path itself did not record the actual caller. If the caller read a similarly named value from another queue, keep the record under the actual object and do not continue using the branches here.

## Sampling Times

Each index value must be followed by a timing label that can be verified:

| Label | What it can establish | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before waiting | The read occurs before entering the wait | Cannot represent the producer state during the wait |
| While waiting | The read occurs within the waiting window described in the report | Cannot establish on its own who blocked progress |
| After waiting | The read occurs after the wait operation or the return | Cannot establish retroactively that nothing changed during the wait |
| Unknown | All that is known is that the value appeared in the record | Cannot be used to compare before-and-after states |

If the code uses `lvProducerIndex`, record it by that name; do not shorten it to "producer index". This read method is suitable for recording the raw producer index observed during a blocking consumer reservation. It provides a sampling point, not a snapshot containing the waiting state, the consumption result, and all adjacent operations.

One value is obtained before the wait, and only afterward does the consumer enter the wait; another value is obtained after the return, and equality of the two values does not fill in what happened in between. Equal numeric values only show that the two sampling points yielded the same value. If the two values differ, that also only establishes a difference between the sampling points; the difference alone cannot identify what happened on the producer or consumer side.

If the report only says "the consumer did not return", preserve the scope of that statement as written. Do not change it to "the consumer will never be woken up", and do not infer "the producer never advanced" from a single value. If the report says "read after entering the wait", also confirm whether the read actually occurred within the same operation; whenever the call site and wait boundary do not line up, return to "Unknown".

## Branches and Stopping Points

### Only One Index Value

Record the value, the object being read, and whatever timing the reader can provide. If the timing is unknown, explicitly write "Unknown". This branch stops here: do not infer a backlog from the magnitude of the value, and do not ask anyone to guess the queue's stage from its magnitude. To continue, just add the call site and one adjacent queue operation; there is no need to fill in the entire call chain first.

### Two Values, but No Operation Sequence

Keep both original values and the locations where each was recorded. If they are equal, do not write "no progress"; if they differ, do not write "recovered" either. Without the intervening operations, it is impossible to know which part of the wait boundary the comparison spans. If all that can be confirmed is that one value came from before the wait and the timing of the other is unknown, treat this as "partial timing information" and still do not enter the attribution branch.

### Call Site Available, but the Object Is Different

Stop using this page's blocking-index judgments and first refile the record under the actual class name. Similar names, both being array queues, or both containing the word blocking are not evidence that they are the same object. Do not merge ordinary queue access, wrapper-layer access, and wait-related access in this class into one timeline.

### Call Site Available and the Object Is the Same

Confirm whether the read occurs before, during, or after the wait, then record it alongside the adjacent operations. At this point, you can return to the source entry point and inspect the local code around the read; recording "where it was read" and "what was seen afterward" matters more than copying more dependency names. If the user-observed result is still only "stuck", retain the symptom; do not fill in a final cause involving the producer or consumer.

### The Report Mentions an Interruption

Whether the interruption occurred before, during, or after the read must be marked separately. The existing records do not contain enough material to link the interruption directly to a particular index change, so do not substitute the old producer-side judgment for the timing of the interruption. If there is only the statement "exception after interruption", stop at that description of the incident and wait for the actual call and return result; do not rewrite the exception as a fixed recovery path.

## The Old Judgment and the Later Narrowing of Scope

The initial draft treated "no visible change in the producer index during the wait" as the producer side not advancing, and prioritized reviewing producer operations. This branch has not been deleted because it reflects the working habits at the time; however, it is now suitable only as a hypothesis to be verified. It extrapolated two values within the observation window into a judgment about the state of the entire producer side, which was too broad.

The follow-up review first narrowed this down to three separable statements:

1. "The wait did not end" is what the user observed.
2. "Read `lvProducerIndex`" is a fact about the code or the call.
3. "The producer side did not advance" is an attribution that has not yet been fully verified.

These three statements can appear together in the same record, but they are not interchangeable. In particular, the presence of `LockSupport` in the code entry point does not justify rewriting the incident's waiting description as a confirmed parking event; nor does obtaining an index through an iteration operation justify treating it as a sample taken during a blocking wait.

The old page also placed local observations of `Iterator` and waiting behavior under the same "index did not change" branch. The two types of records are now kept separately: objects obtained through iteration or traversal results go under traversal observations; values obtained near blocking operations go under waiting observations; ordinary queue operations retain only their own objects and ordering. This does not add conclusions; it prevents a value of unknown origin from being interpreted repeatedly.

## Format for Supplemental Incident Notes

JCT-213 provide a place to fill in the actual calls, invocation methods, and user-observed results. The following lines can be used for supplemental notes; the original description does not need to be rewritten as a complete incident narrative:

```text
Object: MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue / Not checked
Read: lvProducerIndex / Other name
Timing: Before waiting | While waiting | After waiting | Unknown
Adjacent operation: One known operation; leave blank if none is available
User-observed result: Keep the original wording from the incident
Call site: Confirmed local context; write Not found if unavailable
```

"Not checked" is not a conclusion about the object. Once the call site has been filled in, first check whether the receiver of the read really is `MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue`. If not, move it to the record for the actual class; if so, then check the relationship between the read point and the wait operation. The user-observed result should still retain its original level of detail: if the report says "did not return", record that it did not return; if it says "saw the same value", record the same value. Do not add judgments such as "permanent" or "inevitable" to the incident description.

For adjacent operations, retain only the local context that can be confirmed. There is no need to paste in business calls, thread creation, and the entire call chain. Conversely, do not compress "read before waiting, enter the wait, read after returning" into a single line saying "index unchanged before and after"; that would once again lose the boundaries needed for troubleshooting.

## Entry Points That Must Not Be Conflated

Also retain the respective operation names for ordinary iteration, ordinary enqueue or dequeue operations, blocking waits, and sampling after an interruption.

The following descriptions look similar but require different handling:

- "The indices are equal": a comparison result for two numeric values, which must include sampling times;
- "The queue made no progress": broader in scope, and must specify which operation was observed;
- "The consumer is waiting": a description of the incident state, which cannot on its own identify an index-related cause;
- "The producer side did not advance": an attribution, to be discussed only when the call, timing, and adjacent operations all support it.

The last statement in the old notes is the easiest to copy because it is short and immediately gives a direction for investigation. The problem is that a direction for investigation is not a recovery result. If a new record still lacks a call site, retain "call details need to be added"; if it has only a call site but no user-observed result, retain that gap. This page does not make a determination for either type of record.

## Old Margin Notes Still Retained

- Old margin note: When the index stops, look at producer operations first. —— Retained as an early troubleshooting entry point, not as an attribution.
- Later supplemental note: A single numeric value is not enough; at minimum, the timing of the read relative to the wait must be known. —— This is the narrower approach currently used for verification.
- Unanswered: Who was the actual caller in the most recent report, and was the read result seen before waiting or after returning?

If there is only a source path and no caller, first finish checking the path and class name, then stop. The path is still an entry point, but it does not automatically supply the result the user saw. If later material only adds another index value but still lacks the operation sequence, the page should remain in the state of "two sampling points, process unknown".

# Decision record: parked take strategy

This old decision did not start with an interface inventory. The earliest investigation used `blocking`, `take`, and `interruptedexception` as entry points, then traced the call names back to `jctools-core/src/main/java/org/jctools/queues/MpscBlockingConsumerArrayQueue.java`. The file header offered only a small slice of evidence: `package org.jctools.queues;`, along with `java.util.AbstractQueue`, `java.util.Iterator`, and `java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport`. Those lines were enough at the time to focus attention on the wait path; they were not proof of the queue's semantics as a whole.

The first draft compared two directions. One was to keep checking when `take` had no elements; the other was to park the waiting consumers and then return to the wait path. In the end, no new implementation was added for the first option, and parked take remained the working direction at the time. The reason was straightforward: the existing adjacency to `LockSupport` made parking worth investigating first, while `AbstractQueue` and `Iterator` showed that the outer structure had not been rearranged as a result of this discussion.

The state sketch drawn at the time was rough, intended only to prevent "no elements" and "failed call" from being written up as the same phenomenon:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> WaitPath
    WaitPath --> Parked: No elements in queue
    Parked --> WaitPath: Producer-side progress
    WaitPath --> CallReturned: Successful call
    WaitPath --> FailureRecord: Failed call
```

This diagram preserves the old assessment. It does not establish which piece of code performs the parking or what gets cleaned up after resumption. The first draft had come close to equating "the file imports `LockSupport`" with "the failure is due to a missing wakeup"; that attribution was withdrawn after review. An import can only narrow down where to start reading; it cannot stand in for wait duration, thread state, or the conditions at interruption.

There was another suggestion during review: since the issue had been found through `take`, start by treating all failures as problems with the waiting mechanism. That suggestion was not adopted. At most, the evidence from a successful call could show that it returned an element; the old record did not also preserve the queue state before and after parking, or the point at which resumption occurred. The evidence for failed calls was thinner still: all that was known was that they fell somewhere near the wait path. That does not establish whether there were no elements, no resumption, or state left over after an interrupt.

The scope of the decision was therefore narrowed later. parked take was a historical investigation and implementation choice, not a catch-all explanation for blocking anomalies. Switching back to active checking could, on the surface, avoid the discussion of resumption after parking, but it would change the form of waiting the original approach was intended to handle; retaining parked would first require establishing exactly which step execution stopped at when the failure occurred. There was no evidence to support a performance comparison between the two options, nor to claim that either had already completed compatibility verification, so this page did not broaden the decision into a conclusion about a rework.

JCT-216 later spelled out the gap more concretely: the observable results of one successful call and one failed call need to be recorded separately. This addition did not add logs to the old record; it only clarified the order for revisiting it: first use that Java file to identify the section of the wait path containing the call, then place the return or failure alongside the state at the time. DOC-27 can serve as a supplementary reference for the legacy entry-point migration index; it does not change the old conclusion here about the blocking consumer queue.

The conclusion retained here is to continue treating parked take as the selected direction in this history, while no longer using it as the direct explanation for all wait failures. Until the original results for successful and failed calls have been fully recorded, this page can only help readers find the trade-offs made at the time; it cannot serve as current operating rules.

# Postmortem: Two Versions of the Performance Experiment Record

The incident began with "current revision" records for two revisions placed side by side at the same entry point. The entry point did not distinguish the two records, and only on review did it become clear that the observations for MPMC already differed from the old record. The earliest note only said, "MPMC differs from the old record." At the time, this was treated as a discrepancy in results; no immediate conclusion was drawn that the entry-point records themselves conflicted.

## What Happened

The version left in `docs/adj-jctools-core/incidents/jctools-core-performance-lab-two-record-versions-not-merged.md` was preserved first; the later observation was not used to overwrite the earlier one. Reruns then continued, and chunk rotation was able to recover. This showed that the run was not persistently stuck at the same rotation point, but it did not show that the two revisions had been merged or explain the change in the FIFO witness.

Retries stopped once recovery was observed. The final line of green output initially made people lean toward classifying the issue as a transient fluctuation. Only when the version, request context, and stopping conditions were added during a later handoff was that assessment anchored to its original place in the timeline. Speculation about neighboring services was not included in the cause record.

## Impact Confirmed at the Time

Impact was confirmed only for the current entry point and this MPMC observation: readers could see the status of two different revisions in the same place and treat one of them as the sole record. There was no evidence that all consumers had read the wrong version, nor was there evidence that the discrepancy had spread to other work in the performance lab. The earlier guidance that "once recovery occurs, the current entry point can continue to be used" was therefore not accurate enough, but it remains in the exported old record to help explain why the response stopped at the recovery step at the time.

## Remaining Gaps

Why the FIFO witness changed is still unknown. The recovery of chunk rotation can only be treated as an observation from the incident; it cannot be used to infer a root cause or replace an item-by-item comparison of the two revisions. The scope of adoption is also unknown: the exported material does not say how many readers of the entry point treated which record as the current version.

In later reviews, first separate the two revisions, then determine which record a given output belongs to; do not group them solely by page color or the last successful result. This file remains a reference point for the incident as it stood at the time, and the attachments are still maintained by adj-jctools-core.

# On-call procedure for failed performance experiment runs

When a failed run is handed to you, preserve that run first. Results in the performance lab will be overwritten by later reruns. First record the time shown at the entry point, the current revision, the original input, and the first visible difference; put any screenshots in the same place. Do not start by restarting or refreshing permissions, and do not create a new set of inputs to stand in for the original run.

The old draft's instruction to "continue once you find the Maven reactor" was too imprecise. It is retained here to explain why the first difference was missed at the time. Start at the entry point, compare each item only against the most recent known-good sample, and stop guessing about later stages as soon as the first difference appears. `chunk rotation`, `producer reservation`, published slot, and FIFO witness can serve as labels for the observed state; labels are not causes and must not be used to choose recovery actions.

## Before starting

Confirm two things: this is an existing failed run, not an ad hoc comparison someone wants to try; and the on-call engineer has the original input, not a modified copy with the same name. If either cannot be confirmed, record only the entry point and what is missing. Do not start the comparison.

The entry point is still: `docs/adj-jctools-core/runbooks/jctools-core-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. Old links on the page are only navigation aids; do not treat them as evidence of the run's state. If historical text conflicts with the current entry point, go by the first visible result from the current run and record where the mismatch is.

## First divergence

**Access through the regular entry point is denied outright.** Do not switch to an administrator account to bypass this step. Record where access was denied and the request/run id in JCTA-006; this card needs the point of denial seen by a non-admin. There is no run result to compare at this point, so subsequent conclusions about the revision or FIFO are not supported.

**The entry point opens, but the second result was not retained.** JCTA-004 covers only this gap. First confirm whether the missing item is the second run or the second read; if only the final state remains, leave the missing item blank. This card previously received a misrouted expiry action. Do not treat that action as part of the history of this failure. The card also still lists "the upstream interface owner has not confirmed the input fields" as a blocker, so do not assume the same set of fields was used both times.

**The revisions on the two sides do not match.** Keep this run's input fixed, compare only the `jctools-core-performance-lab` revision on each side, and record which side was read first. Do not update either side while comparing them. JCTA-015 is for preserving this difference; it cannot replace the failed sample itself.

## Once the run has started

Work from the most recent known-good sample toward the failed sample, changing only one condition at a time. The comparison variable may be the input, revision, or status returned by the entry point; before starting, state which one is being changed in this comparison. If the first difference appears at `producer reservation`, stop any further cleanup or retries immediately. The on-call record must clearly state which run this marker came from, which actions were not taken afterward, and who took over reviewing the original input.

If `consumer handoff` does not appear, that is a stopping point, not a signal to "just run it again." After pausing, retain the input and revision from that point. If a rerun is the action being tested, record it as a new comparison; it must not overwrite the initial failure. A green result after cleanup must not be backfilled as the result of the original run either.

## Handoff record

Write the handoff in chronological order; identifying a cause first is not required:

- Where the entry point was opened, and whether the regular entry point was usable;
- The input and revision held fixed for this run;
- The first difference, and the last state that could still be confirmed before it;
- Actions taken and hypotheses already ruled out;
- If `producer reservation` is still in the record, who will continue looking into it;
- Which entry point the next shift should return to, rather than continuing from a retelling in chat.

JCTA-013 is for adding the last state that could be confirmed before the failure. Without that state, do not infer a cause from any label observed after the failure. Restoring service does not mean the cause has been found; this page only covers how to preserve the original evidence, stop, and hand off. Recovery actions are still awaiting validation in the shared environment.

When a run goes beyond the performance lab's own inputs, revisions, and failed samples, stop at that boundary first. If further comparison is needed, preserve this run's evidence and do not mix in results from other projects.

# On-Call Procedure for Failed Performance Experiment Runs

For a failed run in the performance lab, first preserve it as it was when first observed. This procedure covers the specific run that has already started or finished but shows a discrepancy in its results, without combining ad hoc tests, supplementary runs, and later green results into the same captured state. The entry point is still at `docs/adj-jctools-core/runbooks/jctools-core-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`; after entering there, first determine whether the original input, current revision, and first visible result can be retrieved.

If any of these cannot be retrieved, do not fill them in from memory. The page can simply record facts such as "Input missing," "revision not read," or "First result overwritten," and then stop there. The value of a failed run lies in preserving the comparison sequence; replacing the old result with a new run often replaces the first difference as well.

## First establish whether this is the same run

The same name displayed at the entry point is not enough to establish that this is the same run. At the start, record the following side by side: where the original input was obtained, the revision currently read, the status first returned by the entry point, and whether a second read or second run has already occurred. There is no need to turn all the information into a conclusion; what matters on call is that the next person can return to the same point.

If the `jctools-core-performance-lab` revision values on the two sides do not match, first hold the input fixed, then compare only the revision values. JCTA-015 records this comparison relationship. Do not casually update either side after reading a difference, and do not fill a gap with the revision from another run. Preserve which side was read first and whether the other side has yet to be read.

The old draft described `Maven reactor` as the only starting point. This passage remains because early people taking over did use it to find the entry point; however, it is not permission to continue execution. The starting point now is the original input and first discrepancy at the current entry point, and `Maven reactor` is only a piece of text in the old records that helps locate it.

## The standard entry point is inaccessible

If access through the standard entry point is denied, the comparison between runs has not yet begun. Do not switch to an administrator account to continue, because that would change the behavior being verified. Record where access was denied and the request/run id, and add them to JCTA-006. The task on that card is to reproduce the denial point as a non-administrator, so "An administrator can open it" cannot be a closure condition.

In this branch, do not record conclusions about FIFO, chunk, or the consumer. They belong to run results that are not yet visible. You may record the entry point address and the object involved when access was denied, but do not add a speculative root cause. After the standard entry point is restored, reconfirm the original input and revision as well; restoring access does not automatically bring back the previously missing results.

## The missing second result

When the entry point can be opened but the second result has not been retained, first distinguish between there having been no second run and the second read not having been saved. JCTA-004 handles only this gap. If only the final status remains on the page, leave the second-result field blank, and do not infer an intermediate status from the final status.

JCTA-004 once had a due-date action posted to the wrong card; that action does not belong to the same run context as "The second result for the current revision is missing," and cannot be used to explain the change in results. The card also retains the blocking reason that the upstream interface owner has not confirmed the input fields. Therefore, until the fields are confirmed, do not claim that the two reads compare the same content, and do not arrange recovery on that basis.

The comparison can continue up to the first difference that can be confirmed. If only the final status remains for both the normal sample and the failed sample, there is no comparison that can be performed on this page; record the gap and wait for the original results to be restored. Do not invent an intermediate status just to make the handoff record complete.

## Preserve the slot just before failure

There are usually many labels after a failure, while the last confirmable state before the failure is easily overlooked. JCTA-013 is used to fill this slot: work backward from the current entry point and retain only the last state that can be confirmed through it. This may be just a read, a revision, or a return value that is still visible; reconstructing the entire process is not required.

If this slot cannot be filled, explicitly leave it blank in the timeline. The later appearance of `producer reservation` does not establish that some cleanup or switch must have occurred before it. Nor may a green sample from a later rerun be placed before the failure. The on-call page should allow "What happened before the failure is unknown" to be a recorded outcome.

## Work from the normal sample to the first difference

When a comparison is possible, use only the most recent normal sample, and write down the single condition to be changed in this round before starting. The condition can be the input, revision, or status returned by the entry point; choose only one per round. Keep all other conditions unchanged to avoid compressing multiple differences into the single statement "The result changed this time."

First compare whether the entry points are the same, then whether the original input is still the same, and then examine the revision. If the preceding item has not been confirmed, do not jump to the next item to explain performance or queue behavior. Once the first difference appears, stop expanding the scope of the comparison. Stopping is not giving up, but preventing later reruns from obscuring the divergence already identified.

When terms such as `chunk rotation`, FIFO witness, or published slot appear in the captured state, record where they appear exactly as shown. They can help the next shift locate the displayed content, but they are not a glossary of causes provided by this page. Different runs may use the same label but stop at different points, so labels must be considered together with the input, revision, and first discrepancy.

The old version stated "Do not clear the run state after seeing producer reservation" very briefly; this update adds specific stopping instructions: preserve the original input, current revision, location where the marker appeared, and actions already performed before that point, then stop cleanup, restarts, or reruns that overwrite the results. If the current shift has already done any of these, record that accurately as well, and do not rewrite the results to make it look as though they were not done.

## `producer reservation` branch

`producer reservation` is a marker in the captured state that must be preserved, not a signal to continue execution. After it appears, first record which run it belongs to, which entry point it was seen through, and what the first difference before it was. Do not extract it on its own from logs or screenshots and hand it to the next shift without the run context.

At this point, do not clear the run state, do not delete this run because "It looks normal after recovery," and do not write a later new run back into the original results. If a new comparison must be started, create a separate record, and note in the new record that it was started after the original state was preserved. The input, revision, and results of the original captured state and the new comparison must not overwrite one another.

At handoff, specify who will continue examining this marker; if no one has taken it over yet, write "Not taken over" as well. Do not call an unspecified reviewer the owner. The goal here is to let the next shift know which run still contains the reservation, not to make judgments about the implementation on the on-call page.

## `consumer handoff` does not appear

If `consumer handoff` does not appear, stop at that step. Preserve the current input, current revision, and point reached in the comparison, and do not keep trying other entry points to make it appear. This stopping point comes from early records of the captured state and still applies: the absence of a displayed handoff should not be treated as a gap that "Another run will fill."

If the rerun itself is the action to be validated, it must be a separate comparison. State in the new record what the single changed condition is, and leave the original run unchanged. A new run turning green describes only the result of the new run, and does not change the fact that handoff was missing from the original run.

If handoff appears but there was already an earlier difference, stop at that earlier point as well. Organize the on-call page around the first divergence, not around whichever label looks more prominent. This lets the person taking over review the comparison sequence, rather than pick an explanation from a series of subsequent observations.

## Recovery already performed and recovery not yet validated

Recovery actions in the shared environment have not yet been established as reusable steps. The TODO from the old version remains in effect: do not treat a judgment made in a personal environment as recovery already validated in the shared environment. The failed run must be preserved first, and whether recovery was attempted, who attempted it, and what the entry point displayed afterward must each be recorded under this run.

Being able to read the entry point after recovery does not mean the second result has been restored; the standard entry point being usable does not mean the revision discrepancy has disappeared either. For every state that "Looks fixed," return to its corresponding branch: for entry point access denial, see JCTA-006, for a missing second result, see JCTA-004, for mismatched revision values on the two sides, see JCTA-015, and for a missing pre-failure state, see JCTA-013.

Do not tie recovery actions to root causes. There is not enough evidence here to prove that any of `chunk rotation`, FIFO witness, published slot, or `producer reservation` is the cause. They can only serve as locator terms within this run; when an explanation is needed, first confirm whether the item occurred before the first difference.

## How to write the handoff

Write the handoff record in chronological order, without starting with a summary. It is recommended to begin with "Whether the entry point is available," followed by the original input, the revision read, whether a second result exists, the last confirmed state before failure, and the first difference. Then list the actions already performed and those not performed, and finally specify the entry point the next shift should open.

You can use the following short format directly:

- Run: whether the original input is preserved; whether the first result is still present.
- Entry point: the standard entry point is available, access is denied, or availability is not yet confirmed.
- Comparison: what the most recent normal sample is; what the single changed condition is in this round.

- Takeover: which section of `docs/adj-jctools-core/runbooks/jctools-core-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md` to return to and continue from.

JCTA-013 only fills in the last confirmable state before failure. JCTA-015 only preserves the comparison of the revision values on the two sides with the same input. The cards help the person taking over find the gaps, but do not replace the input, first result, and stopping point in this run record.

A single run may involve multiple cards, but do not merge them into one overall status. First record the run sequence on this page, then write each gap back to its corresponding card. If a card has no corresponding evidence from the captured state, it is better not to update it. This way, when the second result or pre-failure state is restored later, it will still be clear which blank it fills.

Before finally leaving the run state, confirm that the original input, current revision, first result, and stopping point have not been overwritten by subsequent operations. # Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally addressed a very narrow situation: a quality signal was not progressing as seen from the current entry point, and the aim was to route it to jctools-experimental-quality-signal, an exit action, or the permissions owner. Several later reruns broke "stuck" down into several different cases, but the old branches were not deleted, so when taking over, do not treat the entire page as a finalized, current runbook.

First find the first visible result. This is not the result of the latest run, nor the green status displayed on the page later; it should be possible to place it alongside the input, version, and path used to reach that entry point at the time. If any of these three categories is missing, take the collection branch. The collection branch is only responsible for gathering the missing raw material, and must not supply a cause based on experience when material is missing.

```text
Stuck or failed as seen from the current entry point
├─ First raw result unavailable
│  ├─ No execution trace: collect the missing material, stop
│  └─ Only the page status remains: preserve the page status, still stop
└─ First raw result available
   ├─ No corresponding version identifier
   │  └─ First separate objects with the same name, do not merge results
   └─ Version identifier available
      └─ Compare with the most recent normal sample for the first visible difference
         ├─ No difference
         │  ├─ Check whether the entry points are the same
         │  └─ Check permissions or indexes; stop if still unclear
         └─ Difference found
            ├─ The difference is within the project's own tests, spec, or quality signal records
            │  └─ Keep it within the project, with the person on duty continuing
            └─ The difference extends beyond the current entry point
               └─ Preserve the originals, hand off to the permissions owner or an adjacent maintenance entry point
```

"Having a result" here does not mean that someone says they ran it. The history in JCTB-008 makes this boundary very clear: until collection or execution is confirmed to have actually happened, the current revision remains unknown. Even if the page has a seemingly complete object name, that cannot be used to fill in the version. JCTB-007 address precisely the case of same-name jctools-experimental-quality-signal: versions in references must be clearly labeled, old objects must be kept separate, and two occurrences must not be joined into one just because the names match.

## What to Save First

When a failure occurs, first save the original input, first output, version identifier, and exit point. The input can be the material used for test or spec at the time; if it is no longer available, record it as missing, and do not replace it with input generated next time. For the output, keep the first visible content, and store later revised results separately. For the version, write only a confirmed identifier; if it cannot be confirmed, write unknown until there is evidence of collection or execution.

This step may seem slow, but it addresses the two points in time most easily conflated on the page: the first result after the change, and the result obtained from a later rerun. The case in JCTB-006 requires finding the first post-change result at the current entry point, which later green results must not overwrite. If the first result still exists and later results turn green, save both side by side; green only shows that the later round was green, and cannot rewrite the previous round as a pass.

A rerun by someone other than the author is a separate timeline. JCTB-005 required someone who had not participated in the change to run the original steps, with the author's results used only for comparison; the card later included a quality reproduction record. JCTB-008 also recorded that the non-author's run reached the exit point with an exit code that was not zero, and linked the exit point and nonzero exit code back to the original job. When taking over, first check whether they refer to the same job, the same version, and the same input. If even one of these differs, preserve them separately, and do not erase the differences with the term "reproduction".

## Branch One: No Raw Material

When there is no first record, first check for actual traces of collection or execution. Having only a page name, a person's account, or the final summary status still means material is missing. Record the currently visible entry point and the missing items, then stop. Do not infer the test layering from the quality signal's name, and do not infer the failure location from the exit action's name.

If the collection action has already happened but the results were not attached back to the original job, first retrieve the record of that action. If it cannot be found, preserve the gap of "execution occurred, results not retrieved", and do not treat a blank as a pass. If even whether execution occurred is unconfirmed, continue to keep current revision unknown. Do not perform recovery retries here; the premature retry in the old records has already shown that retrying makes the first observed state harder to identify.

## Branch Two: Material Exists but Versions Are Mixed Together

Objects with the same name, old pages, and current pages can appear at the same time. First check the referenced version identifiers, then check whether they point to the same entry point. If there are no identifiers, record them separately as two objects, and do not carry an old version's green status over to the current revision or backfill the current failure into the old records.

If both sides use the same name but have different exit actions, preserve both results and note their respective entry paths. JCTB-006 recorded the same person on duty specifying different actions to take at expiry on the two sides; this is not sufficient reason to close the branch, but an indication that the objects or entry points on the two sides are not yet aligned. Here, only check the original records and versions, and do not explain the differences in actions on behalf of the person on duty.

## Branch Three: The First Result Differs from the Normal Sample

Compare only the first visible difference. You can first check whether the inputs are the same, then check the versions and entry points, and finally check whether the quality signal records come from the same project. Do not change multiple conditions at once; if conditions change simultaneously, the tree stops here, and retain "unable to normalize for comparison".

If the difference still falls within jctools experimental · Quality Signal Board's own tests, spec, resources, permissions, indexes, or attribution of unstable signals, stop at that node within the project. Here, you can hand the first sample, version, and rerun results to the person on duty, but cannot decide a new exit criterion for the project. The project has its own maintainers, schedule, and exit criteria, and the page status itself does not mean the exit criteria have been met.

If the difference extends beyond the current entry point, or requires changing the behavior consumers see, stop using this page. Hand off the original input, version, first result, rerun results, and exit point together; do not forward only a description saying "it failed". If permissions are missing, hand off to the permissions owner; if records from an adjacent entry point are missing, stop at the current node and raise the question. Do not jump to the final cause without new evidence.

## Old Wording and Later Notes

The early version described the troubleshooting order very briefly: first look at the visible symptoms, then follow one branch to the first place that needs new evidence. That version also retained a recovery action that had not been tried in the shared environment. This limitation still applies; later reruns have not given this page a conclusion about recovery in the shared environment.

The second version added two areas prone to misinterpretation. One is treating the green status after a rerun as recovery of the original state, and the other is inferring intermediate behavior from averages, directory names, or the final display. Both can help locate the issue, but cannot overwrite the first failed sample. The second version also put the non-author rerun, exit point, and nonzero exit code back on the original job, showing that "someone reran it" and "the original job's first result has been explained" are two different things.

The third version retains these old paragraphs, but separates versions sharing the same name, the current revision, and the first post-change result. Some terms in the old paragraphs are still the working terminology used at the time, so read them in their original historical context, and do not elevate them into fixed steps that all quality signals must go through today. The page may still be referenced, so the old branches are not deleted; but it is not the place to make final decisions on behalf of project maintainers.

## Short Path When Taking Over

First open `docs/adj-jctools-experimental/runbooks/jctools-experimental-quality-signal-escalation-contacts-when-stuck.md` and confirm which version of the object you are viewing. Then find the first result at the current entry point; if there is none, return to the collection branch. Once found, check the version identifier, entry path, and exit point, then compare with the most recent normal sample for the first difference. If the comparison leads inside the project, hand it to the person on duty, and if it reaches a permissions or entry-point boundary, stop and hand off to the corresponding entry point.

JCTB-005, JCTB-006, JCTB-007, JCTB-008 are navigation aids for reviewing the cases, not interchangeable conclusions. JCTB-005 show that a non-author rerun had been required for comparison; JCTB-006 preserve the boundary that the first post-change result cannot be overwritten by later green results; JCTB-007 are a reminder to separate objects with the same name by version; JCTB-008 retain the records that current revision remains unknown until confirmed, and that the exit point and nonzero exit code were linked back to the original job. Each supports only its own passage.

The questions still unanswered are: whether the recovery action in the shared environment has actually been completed, and whether the first failed sample can still be preserved after completion. Until both records are available, do not change the page to mark recovery complete, and do not describe unknown items as having satisfied the exit action.

Identify the person based on which object the issue falls on, not by assigning it to whoever replied most recently. The project intake handles intake and handoff; the module maintainer handles samples that have already appeared in the quality signal dashboard; the original owner explains interface behavior; the decision-maker handles scope, authorization, and risk. The blank slots below are intentional; do not fill them with the on-duty person's name before confirmation.

|---|---|---|---|
| `adj-jctools-experimental-temporary handoff boundary` project intake | Project on-call intake | Collect the entry point, time, and minimum symptom, and complete the handoff | Long-term behavior explanation for the quality signal dashboard |
| `published slot`'s expiration action | Temporary maintainer | Handle only the expiration handling for the exit action | Decision of the long-term owner for the published slot |
| Behavior explanation for `jctools-experimental-quality-signal` | Original owner | Explain existing samples, regression stratification, and what unstable signals mean | Temporary maintainer's on-call judgment |
| `atomic generator` | Pending confirmation | Retain the operational label for now | Do not treat a bypass name as an ownership assignment |
| `bounded wait` | Caller or corresponding module maintainer | Provide the call site and minimum symptom | Project intake must not substitute for a subject-matter conclusion |

The project intake is only a routing point. After the temporary maintainer receives the expiration action for `published slot`, they can confirm whether the action is already due and return the entry point and observations to the appropriate place; if the issue turns into a behavior explanation, sample meaning, or long-term interface decision, stop here and return to the original owner. The behavior explanation for jctools-experimental-quality-signal still goes back to the original owner, and the blank remains visible. The most recent replier doesn't automatically become the owner.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Actual user] --> E[Project intake]
    E --> P{Which segment is the object in}
    P --> S[published slot expiration action]
    P --> Q[quality signal behavior]
    P --> A[atomic generator]
    S --> T[Temporary maintainer handles exit action]
    Q --> O[Back to original owner]
    A --> K[Keep blank and route to pending-confirmation entry]
    T --> X[Send back action-completion or expiration information]
    O --> X
```

A handoff carries only three things: the original entry point, the time the result was observed, and the minimum symptom needed for the next person to locate it. If the original input, version, and first visible result are available, retain those too; don't make the questioner rewrite the whole sequence of events. The project intake can coordinate the time window, but it does not explain samples on behalf of the module maintainer or confirm scope on behalf of the decision-maker. When crossing the current interface, record "where it was routed" and "what is still missing"; do not turn unconfirmed items into conclusions.

### Old Labels Still on the Table

The three names from v1 will still appear in searches and old records. The long-term handoff person for `published slot` has not been confirmed, so no name is entered in the table. `atomic generator` was once put in the same table, but there isn't enough material to map it to a maintainer; it is now only a searchable operational label. `bounded wait` still needs the caller to provide a name and entry point. None of these may be used as the basis for "Whoever handled it most recently is responsible."

The project's behavior documentation and temporary handoff documentation are stored separately. `DOC-33` remains the navigation point for quality signal dashboard troubleshooting records; this page keeps who handles what and what to include in a handoff, rather than copying the behavior explanation again. The current handoff entry point is `docs/adj-jctools-experimental/ownership/adj-jctools-experimental-interim-ownership-boundary.md`; the body and attachments are still maintained by `adj-jctools-experimental`.

This indicates that what the handoff recipient received may not be the same version as the description on the card; when receiving the handoff, keep the original input you have separate from the card description, and do not automatically change the owner based on that. The card is for navigation only and cannot fill in the missing long-term owner for this mapping table.

JCTB-016 was initially associated with the support context, then reassigned to the current module maintainer because the person taking it over had reviewed the existing implementation. This reassignment only indicates that, at the time, someone familiar with the implementation needed to continue looking at it; it does not mean that person has permanent authority to interpret `jctools-experimental-quality-signal`. Legacy entry point ─────────────> Current entry point

```text
Entry point: Legacy entry point -----------------> Current entry point
Artifact: Old artifact version ---------------> New artifact version (pending verification)
Rollback: Legacy entry point <------------------- Restore point within the rollback window
```

The mixed display of old and new versions retained in JCTD-009 is one such case: split them by revision first, then check their respective old links and replacement locations.

The old procedure was to copy the link to the current entry point first, then switch one caller that could be found to it; next, check the artifact version produced by the build queue, and finally try returning to the legacy entry point within the rollback window. # Release-window build feedback notes

This review starts by separating the two actions under discussion: keeping the existing atomic-generation entry point, and adjusting the release window before integration. The first remains the known starting point for replay; the second is a window arrangement to compare. They must not be recorded as a single generation failure just because both appear in preparations for the same release.

Earlier failure records put queue state and release-side materials on the same line. This masks the divergence that occurred first: a run may first show a queue-state difference, with missing build materials in the window discovered only later. The latter only shows that the release evidence is incomplete; it cannot establish a concurrency-related cause for the earlier difference. Conversely, discovering missing release materials first does not establish that the queue state was already abnormal.

Keep two short records, following the order events were observed. Start the queue record at the source-code entry point, documenting the difference observed in that actual run and whether it preceded the subsequent release actions. The release record should contain only whether build artifacts were produced and whether the materials in the window were complete. Both records may refer to the same run, but must not be spliced together into a causal chain.

We are keeping the entry point not because it has been proven suitable for every window, but because it is the only one that currently links to a replayable run. If we change the entry point first just to tidy up the window schedule, the generation path and release arrangements will change at the same time; when the next difference appears, we will not be able to tell whether the entry-point change or the window change caused the difference in observations.

# Build Decision Record for the Release Window

At the start of the review, the release window and queue state were treated as two separate areas of recordkeeping. The atomic-generation entry point was still used to return to the generation-side state; the release side kept only the candidate artifact and materials related to that build. Combining the two into a single conclusion would mean writing up a reproducible state as the build already being stable, leaving no reliable starting point for subsequent concurrency explanations.

There were two options on the table. The first was to keep the existing entry point, run generation within the existing window, and attach results from one real run to each candidate artifact brought into the discussion. The second was to adjust the window first, bring generation, execution, and release materials into the same round, and then decide whether to keep the entry point. The latter looked tidier, but at the time there was no material showing which type of failure it could reduce; it might instead obscure where failing samples first appeared.

The decision was to adopt the first option. The window would not be rescheduled for this review, and the existing entry point would remain in use. Samples brought into the discussion were to have two separate records: one for reproducible queue state and another for release evidence. The former could be replayed via the entry point; the latter showed only what that build left behind. Every conclusion had to be replayable via the source-code entry point and one real run, but the two records could not substitute for each other.

For failing samples, preserve the first divergence. Even if a later rerun succeeds, it must not be used to recast the earlier failure as a fluke; first check where the earliest queue state and release materials each began to diverge. This is not about assigning every failure a fixed generation or build label, but about avoiding treating two sources as the same cause when the evidence is insufficient.

The scope approved in this review was also narrow: candidate artifacts had to have a clearly defined queue state, be traceable back to the entry point, and be comparable against an actual run. Results missing any one of these were not to be considered in the window assessment; concurrency explanations could not be used to fill the gaps. This cutoff mattered more at the time than expanding the candidate set, because the expanded comparison would have no common starting point.

One proposal was to classify generation failures directly under the build window, on the grounds that both usually surfaced in the same round. That attribution was not adopted. A failure might first occur in the generated artifact, or might only become visible at runtime; the available records were insufficient to combine them into a single category. Another proposal was to keep only the last successful run to make release decisions easier. This was also rejected because it would lose the first divergence, making it impossible afterward to distinguish changes in queue state from changes in window conditions.

Reservation: not rescheduling the window was a trade-off specific to this review, not a long-term rule. It depended on the existing entry point still being able to provide replayable state, and on release materials being stored separately. After changes to the entry point or release method, this separation might no longer apply; however, retaining both the first divergence and successful samples was still the basis at the time for ruling out incorrect attribution.

The results observed during the maintenance window were not as originally planned. The earliest record did not describe the interface as unavailable. It recorded only a deviation: the constructor compatibility matrix available at the time could not explain the results observed during the window.

Work under the original plan was first halted, and a temporary recovery was performed so observation could continue within the window. The post-recovery state and the assessment of the cause were not documented together. The initial search started with ProxyChannelFactory and the call name. These were simply search entry points close to what was observed at the time. Seeing the construction method at the call site does not mean its relationship to blocking behavior is already understood; this record also did not check whether existing callers were still operating under the pre-window assumptions.

| Comparison item | Status recorded at the time |
| --- | --- |
| Original construction method | Already in the compatibility matrix; still needs review |
| Construction method observed during the window | Recorded; cause not attributed |
| Behavior after temporary recovery | Observation can continue |
| Caller choice | Unconfirmed |

Impact has only been confirmed for this maintenance window. There is no material supporting a broader claim about all blocking interfaces, nor any material showing that the cause was already known during recovery.
